claims.text: French files on Ben Barka. Roughly 1,800 acknowledged CIA documents. Spanish acknowledgement of systematic chemical use, refused by parliamentary vote in 2007. These are questions with answers that someone possesses.

Hassan I appointed him his representative over the Saharan territories by dahir. The date is disputed — 1879 and 1887 both appear in reference literature of comparable authority. The 1887 dating links the appointment to Spanish occupation at Dakhla; the 1879 dating places it earlier and independent of it. This is not a trivial discrepancy: it changes whether the appointment was a reaction to European encroachment or a prior assertion of Moroccan sovereignty, which is exactly the point at issue in the modern territorial argument. Under Abdelaziz, and more clearly under Abdelhafid, the relationship continued: he received arms and subsidies from Fez and Marrakech and acted as the Makhzen's instrument against French advance from Mauritania and Senegal.
what "khalifa" delegated. Two defensible readings:

Qadiriyya-Fadiliyya lineage; substantial scholarly output; founded Smara; appointed khalifa of the Sahara by Hassan I in 1887; organised Saharan resistance to French expansion; moved north in 1910, was defeated, and died at Tiznit on 23 October 1910; his son al-Hiba took Marrakech in 1912 and lost at Sidi Bou Othmane.
his authority rested primarily on religious and scholarly standing, with Makhzen investiture as reinforcement rather than foundation.

the nature of the khalifa relationship; the year of his appointment (1879 vs 1887); any 1910 claim to the sultanate; Spanish arms supply; his birth year (1830 or 1831; one account gives c. 10 February 1830).

the scale of his following, his finances, and the content of his own extensive writings — which exist, are catalogued in part, and have not been used here. Given that he was a prolific author, using European reports about him in preference to his own texts is a methodological failure this dossier is currently committing and flags as such.

Born Rabat 1920; among the youngest signatories of the Independence Manifesto, 11 January 1944; tutor to the future Hassan II; left Istiqlal on 25 January 1959 and helped form the UNFP; secretary and chair of the preparatory commission for the Tricontinental Conference (Havana, January 1966); abducted in Paris on 29 October 1965 in an operation involving French police officers; never seen again.

A 1967 French trial convicted two officers of kidnapping. The court identified Moroccan Interior Minister Mohamed Oufkir as principally responsible. The witness Georges Figon, who testified that Oufkir stabbed Ben Barka, was found dead — officially suicide.

Ahmed Dlimi requesting the operation on the king's behalf. Mossad locating him and supplying logistics (Ronen Bergman, 2018) — JOURNALISTIC, based on Israeli sources. Czechoslovak StB contact 1961–1965 (Jan Koura, 2020) — ACADEMIC, from StB files, and it complicates the martyrology without touching the responsibility question.
The location of the body; the manner and exact date of death; whether Hassan II gave a direct order; the full extent of French and American foreknowledge.

Zaian qaid by Makhzen investiture under Hassan I; led Zaian resistance from 1914; commanded at El Herri 13 Nov 1914; his sons submitted June 1920; he died in the Middle Atlas in early 1921; organised Zaian resistance ended Sept 1921.
his authority was confederal and negotiated, not autocratic; French estimates of his strength are unreliable in both directions.
appointment date; birth year; the fratricide; the claim that he advised his sons to submit.

almost everything about his internal politics — how decisions were taken in the Zaian jemāʿa, how he financed the war, what he thought he was fighting for in his own words. No Zaian-side written source has been used in this dossier. Whether one exists is itself an open question worth pursuing in the Arabic manuscript collections at Rabat.
